Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures & bcdedit /set default recoveryenabled no]', 'MDATP', 'Microsoft', '7d47542a-7c5a-4fd4-85f2-640f2bf0927b_1', '37ed1840-2428-9ace-8db4-fc7ceeda30b9', '', '', 'WindowsDefenderAtp', '', '', 'False', '2024-06-20 09:10:49.054537+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:10:51.876113+00:00', '2024-06-20 09:19:23.179872+00:00', '["1. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('80a1b808-56fb-a977-ce72-b76acd95e64f', 'Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

('65e0e94f-36d8-f3a7-039e-c1770857c3ce', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures ('37ed1840-2428-9ace-8db4-fc7ceeda30b9', 'System recovery setting tampering', 'System recovery setting tampering has been observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures ('e8726a31-a306-23e1-4284-23403d4bd463', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', question_dict.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is a credential theft tool that can harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. 1. Locate the process that is related to the alert. Inspect parent processes and why they were launched.
2. Take note of the name of the remote device and the command that might have been executed.
3. Verify the unusual system activity with system owners.​
4. Check files for prevalence, their locations, and digital signatures.​
5. Check the timeline of both the devices for other suspicious activities around the time of the alert.
6. Submit relevant files for deep analysis and review file behaviors. ​

B. Scope the incident.
1. Find related alerts and activities on both devices. Find out whether they are part of a wider incident in the incident graph.
2. Identify unexpected processes, check suspicious files for prevalence, location and digital signature, submit for deep analysis to inspect behaviors.
3. Identify communications to devices, network addresses, and domains. Verify unusual activities with device owners. Check reputation of URLs and websites.

C. Contain and mitigate the breach.
1. If activity on any of the involved devices is unexpected, isolate the device to prevent the threat from progressing.

Based on my investigation of the database, I found that:

1. **WMI Process Creation Alert**: A suspicious WMI process creation was detected at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.378778+00:00. This represents malware attempting to use WMI (Windows Management Instrumentation) to spawn new processes, which is a known technique to break process trees and evade detection.

2. **Primary Refresh Token (PRT) Access Attempt**: During the same incident timeframe, a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected. The PRT is a critical Azure AD authentication artifact - a JSON Web Token (JWT) that enables single sign-on (SSO) across applications on Windows 10+ devices, iOS, and Android. Attackers targeting this token aim to achieve lateral movement and credential theft.

3. **browsercore.exe Correlation**: The investigation points to **browsercore.exe** running at the specified time (2024-07-04 22:35:03.378778+00:00) as the process of interest. This process should be further scrutinized because:

   - It occurred during the same incident window as the PRT access attempt
   - browsercore.exe is a legitimate Microsoft Edge browser component, but its execution via WMI spawning is highly suspicious
   - The combination of WMI process creation + browsercore.exe execution + PRT access attempt suggests a coordinated attack attempting to:
     * Use WMI to break the process tree and evade detection
     * Leverage browsercore.exe (which has access to browser credentials and tokens) to attempt PRT theft
     * Achieve lateral movement and credential compromise

question_dict.question: Related to this alert, there was also an incident where file backups were deleted. Can you identify the command used in the process that deleted the file snapshots and shadow copies?
solution: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected for the AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
File backups, including all snapshots and shadow copies, were deleted using process `7236` at `2024-06-20t09:10:51.2193152z` with the command line `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`.

info.submitted_answer:
The command used to delete file snapshots and shadow copies is: **vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all**

This command deletes all Volume Shadow Copies (VSS snapshots) on the affected systems. The command was executed with high privilege elevation through the WMI Provider Host (wmiprvse.exe) process, and was deployed across multiple machines in the environment (vnevado-win10s, vnevado-win10r, vnevado-win11t, vnevado-win11u) on June 20, 2024, starting around 09:10 UTC. This is consistent with the Iranian MOIS wiper malware activity described in the threat report, which opportunistically deployed destructive capabilities in response to the Israel-Hamas conflict.

The command used is: **`vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`**

This command is executed through the VSSADMIN.EXE tool (Volume Shadow Copy Service Administration tool). The process shows:
- Process Name: vssblatemp.exe
- Parent Process: wmiprvse.exe (WMI Provider Host)
- Command Line: `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`
- Elevation: High privilege execution
- Multiple executions across different machines (vnevado-win10s, vnevado-win10r, vnevado-win11t, vnevado-win11u)

This is a destructive command that deletes all Volume Shadow Copies (VSS snapshots) on the system, which is a common technique used by wiper malware to prevent system recovery and backup restoration.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
